paper.title: The gift of time? School starting age and mental health
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement. The acknowledgements state: …

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC), fifth and sixth survey waves
registers.years: women pregnant 1996-2002; fifth wave at child age 7 and sixth wave at child age 11
registers.role: outcomes (the 25-item SDQ at ages 7 and 11), treatment (school starting age, from the fifth-wave question on when the child started kindergarten), sample frame, and pretreatment 18-month developmental measures
variables_mentioned: can keep occupied for 15 min aged 18m

registers.role: treatment assignment and sample frame: the child's exact date of birth (the forcing variable), birth weight, origin, gender, gestational age
controls: parents' gross annual income (measured in 1,000 DKK and adjusted to the 2010 level using the consumer price index)
controls: parents' educational attainment (years of schooling)
descriptive validation of the SDQ in Table 9: ADHD diagnoses based on ICD-10 codes F900, F901, F908, F909 and F989
linkage: used together with the registers to identify the day of birth and school starting age of DNBC children

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish National Tests (reading and mathematics)
registers.role: descriptive validation of the SDQ (Table 9, panel C; the underlying regressions are 'available on request')

linkages: DNBC children matched to data for the full Danish population from the national administrative registers, linked by a unique personal identifier hosted at Statistics Denmark
day of birth and school starting age identified by matching DNBC data to population data in the Danish administrative registry and Ministry of Education records

children linked to parents and siblings after adjusting the birth year to run from July to June instead of January to December (e.g. children born July 2000 to June 2001 are merged to parents' characteristics for January to December 1999)
DNBC data linked to hospital records on ADHD diagnoses, and to Danish National Test scores, for the descriptive validation in Table 9

sample.universe: children in the Danish National Birth Cohort (a nationwide cohort of women pregnant 1996-2002, roughly 10% of births in the population in that period; nearly 93,000 women participated in the baseline interviews), linked to the full Danish population registers
selection_rules: child included in the DNBC and observed in the fifth (age 7) and/or sixth (age 11) survey wave
born within the 30-day window on each side of the January 1 school-entry cutoff (the forcing variable day_i runs from -30 to +30)
information on school starting age available
a completed SDQ questionnaire either at age 7 or at age 11, or at both ages
for the first-stage, reduced-form and 2SLS estimates: 7,642 children in the age-7 wave and 5,226 in the age-11 wave
for the placebo regressions: 5,946 (5,945 with covariates) children with the 18-month developmental measures available
missing values in covariates are replaced with zeros and indicators for missing variables are included
sample.period: birth cohorts around the turn of each year 1996/97 to 2002/03; survey waves at child ages 7 and 11
sample.n_observations: 8,092 children in the 30-day window (7,642 in the age-7 estimation sample; 5,226 in the age-11 estimation sample); the population comparison in Table 1 has 54,213 children

construction_notes: The forcing variable day_i is the exact birth date relative to the January 1 cutoff: 0, 1, 2, ... for children born January 1, 2, 3, and -1, -2, -3, ... for children born December 31, 30, 29.
School starting age is the age at entry into kindergarten (grade zero, 'Boernehaveklasse'), taken from the fifth-wave question on when the child started kindergarten.

Each SDQ subscore is the sum of five uniquely linked items scored 0, 1 or 2 (range 0-10); the total difficulties score is the sum of the four difficulties subscales (range 0-40); the pro-social scale is measured with the opposite sign.
SDQ scores are standardized using the full population in each survey wave so that coefficients are effect sizes.
Classification thresholds: total difficulties 0-13 normal, 14-16 borderline, 17-40 abnormal; pro-social scale 6-10 normal, 5 borderline, 0-4 abnormal.
Parents' gross income is measured in 1,000 DKK and adjusted to the 2010 level using the consumer price index (Table 1 note).
Parents are defined as non-Western if they are immigrants to Denmark from a non-Western country according to the classification by Statistics Denmark (Table 1 note).
Number of siblings living in the household is recorded when the child is 2 years old; 'nonsingletons' are always defined as having an older sibling (Table 5-7 notes).
Before linking children to parents and siblings the birth year is adjusted to run from July to June.
Missing covariate values are replaced with zeros, with indicators for missing variables included in the regressions.
Robust (heteroscedasticity-consistent) standard errors are reported rather than standard errors clustered on the running variable, because the robust ones are slightly larger in this application.
Tables 5-8 add linear time trends estimated separately on each side of the cutoff; all subgroup sample splits are done at the median.
ADHD diagnoses in Table 9 are based on ICD-10 codes F900, F901, F908, F909 and F989.

claims.statement: Being born on January 1 or later raises school starting age by 0.20 years in the age-7 DNBC sample (the first stage of the fuzzy RD design).

treatment.label: Born on January 1 or later, 1(day_i >= 0) -- the intent to treat (ITT) to a delayed school start

register_source.value: Danish administrative registers (the birth records) and Ministry of Education records, linked by the personal identifier at Statistics Denmark; no register code or variable name is given

definition.value: Indicator for the child's exact date of birth being on or after the January 1 school-entry cutoff. Children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, so school starting age should jump as birthdays change from December 31 to January 1. The forcing variable day_i is the exact birth date relative to the cutoff (January 1 = 0).

timing.value: determined at birth; the assignment is predetermined relative to all outcomes

outcome.label: School starting age (age at kindergarten entry, in years)

register_source.value: DNBC fifth survey wave report of when the child started kindergarten, matched to the administrative registers and Ministry of Education records

definition.value: Age in years at entry into kindergarten (grade zero); children are supposed to enroll in the calendar year in which they turn 6, so compliers born January 1 start one year older than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at kindergarten entry; measured in the DNBC survey

units.value: years of school starting age for children born on January 1 or later (ITT)

magnitude.interpretation: school starting age jumps by 0.18 to 0.20 years at the birth date cutoff; the first-stage F-statistic is 45.418, and the authors note that compliance among children born in December is only partial

estimand.target_population: children in the local DNBC sample born within 30 days of the January 1 cutoff and observed in the age-7 survey wave
estimand.time_horizon: school starting age itself, i.e. measured at kindergarten entry
estimand.formal_query: E[SSA | do(born on or after January 1)] - E[SSA | do(born before January 1)], in the limit at the cutoff

population.description: Children in the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC) born within 30 days before or after the January 1 school-entry cutoff, with information on school starting age and a completed SDQ in the fifth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 7 years old
population.birth_cohorts: children of women pregnant between 1996 and 2002 (DNBC); the population comparison in Figure A1 covers children born in Denmark 1997-2003
population.period: DNBC fifth wave (child aged 7) and sixth wave (child aged 11); survey waves fielded on a rolling basis
population.selection: children enrolled in the DNBC (women pregnant 1996-2002, roughly 10% of births) who responded to the fifth and/or sixth survey wave and have a completed SDQ and school starting age; the survey sample has higher birth weight, fewer non-Western children and more educated, richer and older parents than the population (Table 1), and the authors state the survey data are not representative

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

lhs: born on or after the January 1 cutoff
given: day of birth relative to the January 1 cutoff (smooth function; local sample within 30 days)

implies_edges.from: predetermined child and family characteristics
implies_edges.to: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

implies_edges.from: unobserved determinants of child mental health
implies_edges.to: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: The local linear/polynomial specification in the forcing variable and the 30-day bandwidth are adequate (functional form and bandwidth choice)
key_assumptions.supported_by: results from various specifications and bandwidths (20 to 170 days, first- to third-order polynomials) in Figures A2 and A3

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on participation and response in the DNBC survey waves, which is nonrandom; the authors assume this does not threaten internal validity because participation is balanced at the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure A1 shows no sign of a jump in attrition around the cutoff; participation is balanced around the birthday threshold; the authors concede an external-validity caveat

implies_edges.from: DNBC participation and response in the age-7/age-11 survey wave

key_assumptions.assumption: Mother-reported SDQ ratings are not driven by reference-group (rater) bias, i.e. the ratings are not merely relative to the child's classroom peers
key_assumptions.supported_by: Elder (2010) finds parental assessments are not subject to these biases; the authors also split the sample by whether the child has an older sibling and condition on classmates' average school starting age (Table 7)

threats_discussed: manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 threshold
nonrandom selection into the DNBC survey and nonrandom nonresponse to the last survey waves (external validity)
the ITT contrast conflates a higher school starting age with fewer years of formal schooling at the time of observation
reference-group (rater) bias in mother-reported SDQ ratings
choice of functional form and bandwidth
localness of the RD estimand and the LATE/complier interpretation of the fuzzy design
multiple hypothesis testing across the 12 core outcomes (six SDQ measures at two ages)
robustness_checks: estimates with and without the full covariate set (Table 2 and Table 4, columns 1 and 3 vs 2 and 4)
McCrary density test of the running variable (Figure 2) and histogram of birth dates in survey and population data (Figure A1)
covariate balance regressions (Table A1) and balance of the covariate index predicting each outcome (Table 3)
placebo regressions on pretreatment developmental measures reported at 18 months (Table A2)
bandwidth sensitivity from 20 to 170 days with first-, second- and third-order polynomials (Figures A2 and A3)
sample splits by gender, parental education, parental income and birth weight (Tables 5 and 6)
splits by older-sibling status and a specification conditioning on classmates' average school starting age (Table 7)
binary abnormal and borderline outcomes (Table 8)
complier diagnostics following Bertanha and Imbens (2014) (Figures 5 and 6)
unresolved_confounders: years of formal schooling at the time of observation is collinear with school starting age in the ITT contrast; the authors argue the role of years of schooling can be deprecated rather than ruling it out
possible reference-group (rater) bias in mother-reported SDQ ratings, which the authors assess only indirectly
nonrandom nonresponse to the last DNBC survey waves (respondents tended to be more affluent)

estimator.value: OLS (local linear regression-discontinuity first stage; robust standard errors)

estimation.specification: Equation (2) with school starting age as the dependent variable: an indicator for being born January 1 or later, a smooth function of the day of birth, the full covariate set and birth-year fixed effects, on the local sample of children born 30 days before and after the cutoff
controls: indicators for missing covariate values (missing values replaced with zeros)
estimation.clustering: none; heteroscedasticity-consistent (robust) standard errors are reported. The authors note that Lee and Lemieux (2010) suggest clustering on the running variable but report robust standard errors because these are slightly larger in their case

adjustment_set.label: day of birth relative to the January 1 cutoff (linear splines / smooth function g(day_i))

heterogeneity.finding: the first-stage effect is much smaller for boys (0.12 at age 7, 0.09 at age 11) than for girls (0.27 at age 7, 0.28 at age 11); boys tend to be always-takers so the identifying variation is uniquely relevant for girls (Tables 5 and 6, column 1)
the first stage is 0.18 to 0.20 years in both the age-7 and the age-11 wave and with or without covariates (Table 2, columns 1-4)

population.description: Children in the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC) born within 30 days before or after the January 1 school-entry cutoff, with information on school starting age and a completed SDQ in the sixth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 11 years old
population.birth_cohorts: children of women pregnant between 1996 and 2002 (DNBC); the population comparison in Figure A1 covers children born in Denmark 1997-2003
population.period: DNBC fifth wave (child aged 7) and sixth wave (child aged 11); survey waves fielded on a rolling basis
subgroups_defined: boys vs girls
parental education above vs below the sample median
parental income above vs below the sample median
birth weight above vs below the sample median
children with vs without an older sibling
specification conditioning on classmates' average school starting age
abnormal vs borderline (binary) SDQ ratings
compliers vs never-takers vs always-takers (Bertanha and Imbens, 2014 diagnostic)
population.selection: children enrolled in the DNBC (women pregnant 1996-2002, roughly 10% of births) who responded to the fifth and/or sixth survey wave and have a completed SDQ and school starting age; the survey sample has higher birth weight, fewer non-Western children and more educated, richer and older parents than the population (Table 1), and the authors state the survey data are not representative

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on participation and response in the DNBC survey waves, which is nonrandom; the authors assume this does not threaten internal validity because participation is balanced at the threshold

key_assumptions.assumption: Mother-reported SDQ ratings are not driven by reference-group (rater) bias, i.e. the ratings are not merely relative to the child's classroom peers
key_assumptions.supported_by: Elder (2010) finds parental assessments are not subject to these biases; the authors also split the sample by whether the child has an older sibling and condition on classmates' average school starting age (Table 7)

reference-group (rater) bias in mother-reported SDQ ratings
choice of functional form and bandwidth
localness of the RD estimand and the LATE/complier interpretation of the fuzzy design
multiple hypothesis testing across the 12 core outcomes (six SDQ measures at two ages)
robustness_checks: estimates with and without the full covariate set (Table 2 and Table 4, columns 1 and 3 vs 2 and 4)
McCrary density test of the running variable (Figure 2) and histogram of birth dates in survey and population data (Figure A1)
covariate balance regressions (Table A1) and balance of the covariate index predicting each outcome (Table 3)
placebo regressions on pretreatment developmental measures reported at 18 months (Table A2)
bandwidth sensitivity from 20 to 170 days with first-, second- and third-order polynomials (Figures A2 and A3)
sample splits by gender, parental education, parental income and birth weight (Tables 5 and 6)
splits by older-sibling status and a specification conditioning on classmates' average school starting age (Table 7)
binary abnormal and borderline outcomes (Table 8)
complier diagnostics following Bertanha and Imbens (2014) (Figures 5 and 6)

anchor_quote.text: we find that increasing the school starting age by 1 year reduces inattention/hyperactivity at age 7 by 0.73 SD (i.e., -0.147/0.201)

claims.statement: A 1-year increase in school starting age changes the standardized SDQ inattention/hyperactivity score at age 7 by -0.73 standard deviations.

links.pointer_quote: Interestingly, we find that these effects are largely driven by a large reduction (effect size = -0.73) in a single SDQ construct: the SDQ's inattention/hyperactivity score.

treatment.label: School starting age (age at kindergarten entry, in years)

register_source.value: DNBC fifth survey wave (the respondent was asked when the child started kindergarten), matched to population data in the Danish administrative registers and Ministry of Education records; no register code is given

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten, around age 6 to 6.5 (survey sample mean 6.48 years, SD 0.67)

outcome.label: Standardized SDQ inattention/hyperactivity score at age 7

definition.value: Sum of the five mother-rated SDQ items linked to the inattention/hyperactivity subscale (range 0 to 10), standardized using the full population in each survey wave. The paper describes this construct as effectively synonymous with self-regulation, i.e. a measure indicating a lack of self-regulation.

timing.value: mother-rated in the fifth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 7 years old; raters are asked to consider the last 6 months

units.value: standard deviations of the standardized SDQ score per 1-year increase in school starting age

magnitude.interpretation: we find that increasing the school starting age by 1 year reduces inattention/hyperactivity at age 7 by 0.73 SD (i.e., -0.147/0.201). The authors add that these effect sizes are quite large, particularly for at-scale field settings, and as large or larger than the mental-health gaps by income and gender.

value.normalisation: SSAi is instrumented by 1(day_i ≥ 0); the specification includes the full covariate set, birth-year indicators and linear time trends separate on each side of the cutoff. SDQ outcomes are standardized using the full population in each survey wave, so β1 is an effect size per year of school starting age. The IV estimate equals the ratio of the reduced-form estimate to the first-stage estimate.

boundary_conditions: estimates are defined by variation around the January 1 threshold and are necessarily local; whether the results generalize to those born at other times is uncertain
the DNBC survey sample is not representative of the population and nonresponse to the last waves is nonrandom (respondents tended to be more affluent)
in the fuzzy design the estimates are defined for the subpopulation of compliers, who appear to be distinctive

claims.statement: A 1-year increase in school starting age changes the standardized SDQ peer problems score at age 7 by -0.46 standard deviations among children with birth weight below the sample median.

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

treatment.label: School starting age (age at kindergarten entry, in years)

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten, around age 6 to 6.5 (survey sample mean 6.48 years, SD 0.67)

outcome.label: Standardized SDQ inattention/hyperactivity score at age 7

definition.value: Sum of the five mother-rated SDQ items linked to the inattention/hyperactivity subscale (range 0 to 10), standardized using the full population in each survey wave. identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth
identification.instrument: 1(day_i >= 0), an indicator for being born on January 1 or later, instrumenting school starting age

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

anchor_quote.text: The corresponding two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimate for age 11 is -0.69 SD (i.e., -0.131/0.190).

claims.statement: A 1-year increase in school starting age changes the standardized SDQ inattention/hyperactivity score at age 11 by -0.69 standard deviations.

links.pointer_quote: We find that the large and concentrated effects largely persist to later childhood (i.e., an effect for inattention/hyperactivity of -0.69).

treatment.label: School starting age (age at kindergarten entry, in years)

register_source.value: DNBC fifth survey wave (the respondent was asked when the child started kindergarten), matched to population data in the Danish administrative registers and Ministry of Education records; no register code is given

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten, around age 6 to 6.5 (survey sample mean 6.48 years, SD 0.67)

outcome.label: Standardized SDQ inattention/hyperactivity score at age 11

definition.value: Sum of the five mother-rated SDQ items linked to the inattention/hyperactivity subscale (range 0 to 10), standardized using the full population in each survey wave. The paper describes this construct as effectively synonymous with self-regulation, i.e. a measure indicating a lack of self-regulation.

timing.value: mother-rated in the sixth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 11 years old; raters are asked to consider the last 6 months

units.value: standard deviations of the standardized SDQ score per 1-year increase in school starting age

magnitude.interpretation: The corresponding two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimate for age 11 is -0.69 SD (i.e., -0.131/0.190).. The authors add that these effect sizes are quite large, particularly for at-scale field settings, and as large or larger than the mental-health gaps by income and gender.

claims.statement: A 1-year increase in school starting age changes the standardized SDQ peer problems score at age 11 by -0.31 standard deviations among children whose parents' gross income is below the sample median.

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten, around age 6 to 6.5 (survey sample mean 6.48 years, SD 0.67)

claims.statement: A 1-year increase in school starting age changes the standardized SDQ emotional symptoms score at age 11 by 0.16 standard deviations among children with birth weight below the sample median.

treatment.label: School starting age (age at kindergarten entry, in years)

register_source.value: DNBC fifth survey wave (the respondent was asked when the child started kindergarten), matched to population data in the Danish administrative registers and Ministry of Education records; no register code is given

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten, around age 6 to 6.5 (survey sample mean 6.48 years, SD 0.67)

outcome.label: Standardized SDQ emotional symptoms score at age 11

definition.value: Sum of the five mother-rated SDQ items linked to the emotional symptoms subscale (range 0 to 10), standardized using the full population in each survey wave.

timing.value: mother-rated in the sixth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 11 years old; raters are asked to consider the last 6 months

units.value: standard deviations of the standardized SDQ score per 1-year increase in school starting age

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

key_assumptions.assumption: Mother-reported SDQ ratings are not driven by reference-group (rater) bias, i.e. the ratings are not merely relative to the child's classroom peers

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: school starting age jumps discontinuously for children born January 1 or later (first stage)

implies_edges.from: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: being born January 1 or later affects the SDQ outcomes only through school starting age (in particular not through the fewer years of formal schooling completed at the time the mother rates the child)
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors discuss this threat and argue the role of years of schooling can be deprecated: effects appear on only one SDQ construct, are similar in size at ages 7 and 11, and any bias from years of schooling would work against their finding; no direct test is reported

implies_edges.from: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Parents select into a delayed school start on information unobserved by the researcher (negative selection into treatment), so OLS is biased; the RD design is needed to break this dependence

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth
identification.instrument: 1(day_i >= 0), an indicator for being born on January 1 or later, instrumenting school starting age

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

claims.statement: A 1-year increase in school starting age changes the standardized SDQ inattention/hyperactivity score at age 11 by -1.09 standard deviations among children with an older sibling.

treatment.label: School starting age (age at kindergarten entry, in years)

register_source.value: DNBC fifth survey wave (the respondent was asked when the child started kindergarten), matched to population data in the Danish administrative registers and Ministry of Education records; no register code is given

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten, around age 6 to 6.5 (survey sample mean 6.48 years, SD 0.67)

outcome.label: Standardized SDQ inattention/hyperactivity score at age 11

definition.value: Sum of the five mother-rated SDQ items linked to the inattention/hyperactivity subscale (range 0 to 10), standardized using the full population in each survey wave. The paper describes this construct as effectively synonymous with self-regulation, i.e. a measure indicating a lack of self-regulation.

timing.value: mother-rated in the sixth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 11 years old; raters are asked to consider the last 6 months

units.value: standard deviations of the standardized SDQ score per 1-year increase in school starting age

register_source.value: DNBC fifth survey wave (the respondent was asked when the child started kindergarten), matched to population data in the Danish administrative registers and Ministry of Education records; no register code is given

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten, around age 6 to 6.5 (survey sample mean 6.48 years, SD 0.67)

outcome.label: Indicator for an abnormal SDQ total difficulties rating at age 7

definition.value: Binary indicator for an abnormal rating on the SDQ total difficulties scale at age 7. Each SDQ score can be classified as normal, borderline or abnormal; for the total difficulties score 0-13 is normal, 14-16 borderline and 17-40 abnormal, and for the pro-social scale 6-10 is normal, 5 borderline and 0-4 abnormal.

timing.value: mother-rated in the fifth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 7 years old

units.value: change in the probability of the indicator (0-1 scale) per 1-year increase in school starting age, from a linear probability model

estimand.target_population: compliers in the local DNBC sample with a completed SDQ in the age-7 wave
estimand.compliers: children who comply with the school starting age cutoff; the authors note the printed sample mean is based on the full sample including never takers, who appear to have considerably lower levels of difficulties
estimand.time_horizon: SDQ reported by the mother in the fifth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 7 years old
estimand.formal_query: E[1(abnormal) | do(SSA = s+1)] - E[1(abnormal) | do(SSA = s)] for compliers at the January 1 cutoff

population.description: Children in the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC) born within 30 days before or after the January 1 school-entry cutoff, with information on school starting age and a completed SDQ in the fifth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 7 years old
population.birth_cohorts: children of women pregnant between 1996 and 2002 (DNBC); the population comparison in Figure A1 covers children born in Denmark 1997-2003
population.period: DNBC fifth wave (child aged 7) and sixth wave (child aged 11); survey waves fielded on a rolling basis
subgroups_defined: boys vs girls
parental education above vs below the sample median
parental income above vs below the sample median
birth weight above vs below the sample median
children with vs without an older sibling
specification conditioning on classmates' average school starting age
abnormal vs borderline (binary) SDQ ratings
compliers vs never-takers vs always-takers (Bertanha and Imbens, 2014 diagnostic)
population.selection: children enrolled in the DNBC (women pregnant 1996-2002, roughly 10% of births) who responded to the fifth and/or sixth survey wave and have a completed SDQ and school starting age; the survey sample has higher birth weight, fewer non-Western children and more educated, richer and older parents than the population (Table 1), and the authors state the survey data are not representative

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth
identification.instrument: 1(day_i >= 0), an indicator for being born on January 1 or later, instrumenting school starting age

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

lhs: born on or after the January 1 cutoff
given: day of birth relative to the January 1 cutoff (smooth function; local sample within 30 days)

implies_edges.to: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

implies_edges.from: unobserved determinants of child mental health
implies_edges.to: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: The local linear/polynomial specification in the forcing variable and the 30-day bandwidth are adequate (functional form and bandwidth choice)
key_assumptions.supported_by: results from various specifications and bandwidths (20 to 170 days, first- to third-order polynomials) in Figures A2 and A3

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on participation and response in the DNBC survey waves, which is nonrandom; the authors assume this does not threaten internal validity because participation is balanced at the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure A1 shows no sign of a jump in attrition around the cutoff; participation is balanced around the birthday threshold; the authors concede an external-validity caveat

implies_edges.from: DNBC participation and response in the age-7/age-11 survey wave

key_assumptions.assumption: Mother-reported SDQ ratings are not driven by reference-group (rater) bias, i.e. the ratings are not merely relative to the child's classroom peers
key_assumptions.supported_by: Elder (2010) finds parental assessments are not subject to these biases; the authors also split the sample by whether the child has an older sibling and condition on classmates' average school starting age (Table 7)

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: school starting age jumps discontinuously for children born January 1 or later (first stage)
key_assumptions.supported_by: first-stage estimates of 0.18 to 0.20 years with F-statistics of 22.7 to 45.4 (Table 2) and the graphical first stage (Figure 1); first-stage F-statistics for the excluded instrument are reported in square brackets in Tables 5-7

implies_edges.from: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: being born January 1 or later affects the SDQ outcomes only through school starting age (in particular not through the fewer years of formal schooling completed at the time the mother rates the child)
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors discuss this threat and argue the role of years of schooling can be deprecated: effects appear on only one SDQ construct, are similar in size at ages 7 and 11, and any bias from years of schooling would work against their finding; no direct test is reported

implies_edges.from: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity / the LATE theorem: with heterogeneous effects the 2SLS estimate is the effect for the subpopulation of compliers with their ITT
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors invoke the LATE theorem (Imbens & Angrist, 1994) and examine whether the complier population is distinctive following Bertanha and Imbens (2014) (Figures 5 and 6)

key_assumptions.assumption: Parents select into a delayed school start on information unobserved by the researcher (negative selection into treatment), so OLS is biased; the RD design is needed to break this dependence
key_assumptions.supported_by: OLS estimates of equation (1) suggest children who start school late have substantially higher levels of inattention/hyperactivity (reported in the text, not in a table)

estimation.specification: Fuzzy RD / 2SLS: equation (1) with school starting age instrumented by an indicator for being born January 1 or later (equation (2) as the first stage), with the full covariate set, birth-year fixed effects and linear time trends separate on each side of the cutoff, on the local sample of children born 30 days before and after the cutoff; the dependent variable is a binary indicator for an abnormal (or borderline/abnormal) rating
controls: indicators for missing covariate values (missing values replaced with zeros)
estimation.clustering: none; heteroscedasticity-consistent (robust) standard errors are reported. The authors note that Lee and Lemieux (2010) suggest clustering on the running variable but report robust standard errors because these are slightly larger in their case

the printed mean of this dependent variable is 0.03; across both ages only 5% to 8% of respondents had inattention/hyperactivity ratings that qualified as abnormal or borderline

treatment.label: School starting age (age at kindergarten entry, in years)

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

definition.value: Binary indicator for a borderline (borderline/abnormal) rating on the SDQ inattention/hyperactivity scale at age 7. claims.statement: A 1-year increase in school starting age changes the probability of a borderline/abnormal SDQ pro-social behavior rating at age 7 by -0.11.

treatment.label: School starting age (age at kindergarten entry, in years)

register_source.value: DNBC fifth survey wave (the respondent was asked when the child started kindergarten), matched to population data in the Danish administrative registers and Ministry of Education records; no register code is given

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten, around age 6 to 6.5 (survey sample mean 6.48 years, SD 0.67)

outcome.label: Indicator for a borderline/abnormal SDQ pro-social behavior rating at age 7

definition.value: Binary indicator for a borderline (borderline/abnormal) rating on the SDQ pro-social behavior scale at age 7. Each SDQ score can be classified as normal, borderline or abnormal; for the total difficulties score 0-13 is normal, 14-16 borderline and 17-40 abnormal, and for the pro-social scale 6-10 is normal, 5 borderline and 0-4 abnormal.

timing.value: mother-rated in the fifth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 7 years old

units.value: change in the probability of the indicator (0-1 scale) per 1-year increase in school starting age, from a linear probability model

estimand.target_population: compliers in the local DNBC sample with a completed SDQ in the age-7 wave

estimand.formal_query: E[1(abnormal) | do(SSA = s+1)] - E[1(abnormal) | do(SSA = s)] for compliers at the January 1 cutoff

population.description: Children in the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC) born within 30 days before or after the January 1 school-entry cutoff, with information on school starting age and a completed SDQ in the fifth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 7 years old
population.birth_cohorts: children of women pregnant between 1996 and 2002 (DNBC); the population comparison in Figure A1 covers children born in Denmark 1997-2003
population.period: DNBC fifth wave (child aged 7) and sixth wave (child aged 11); survey waves fielded on a rolling basis

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

claims.statement: Being born on January 1 or later does not shift the covariate-based predicted value of the standardized SDQ total difficulties score at age 11 (covariate balance test).

treatment.label: Born on January 1 or later, 1(day_i >= 0) -- the intent to treat (ITT) to a delayed school start

definition.value: Indicator for the child's exact date of birth being on or after the January 1 school-entry cutoff. Children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, so school starting age should jump as birthdays change from December 31 to January 1. The forcing variable day_i is the exact birth date relative to the cutoff (January 1 = 0).

timing.value: determined at birth; the assignment is predetermined relative to all outcomes

register_source.value: Danish administrative registers (birth records, income registers, education registers) for the covariates; the predicted SDQ value is constructed from the DNBC survey outcome

definition.value: Fitted value from a first-step regression of the SDQ outcome on all covariates (indicators for birth year, age at interview, parents' years of schooling, parents' gross income, parents' age at childbirth, birth weight, gender and origin); it represents an index of all the covariates weighted by their OLS-estimated outcome relevance.

timing.value: covariates are predetermined (measured at or before the child's birth, or at the time of interview for age at interview)

units.value: standard deviations of the predicted (covariate-index) standardized SDQ measure, for children born on January 1 or later

estimand.formal_query: E[X-hat | do(born on or after January 1)] - E[X-hat | do(born before January 1)], in the limit at the cutoff, expected to be zero

population.description: Children in the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC) born within 30 days before or after the January 1 school-entry cutoff, with information on school starting age and a completed SDQ in the sixth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 11 years old
population.birth_cohorts: children of women pregnant between 1996 and 2002 (DNBC); the population comparison in Figure A1 covers children born in Denmark 1997-2003
population.period: DNBC fifth wave (child aged 7) and sixth wave (child aged 11); survey waves fielded on a rolling basis
population.selection: children enrolled in the DNBC (women pregnant 1996-2002, roughly 10% of births) who responded to the fifth and/or sixth survey wave and have a completed SDQ and school starting age; the survey sample has higher birth weight, fewer non-Western children and more educated, richer and older parents than the population (Table 1), and the authors state the survey data are not representative

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

multiple hypothesis testing across the 12 core outcomes (six SDQ measures at two ages)

covariate balance regressions (Table A1) and balance of the covariate index predicting each outcome (Table 3)
placebo regressions on pretreatment developmental measures reported at 18 months (Table A2)
bandwidth sensitivity from 20 to 170 days with first-, second- and third-order polynomials (Figures A2 and A3)
sample splits by gender, parental education, parental income and birth weight (Tables 5 and 6)

binary abnormal and borderline outcomes (Table 8)
complier diagnostics following Bertanha and Imbens (2014) (Figures 5 and 6)

population.period: DNBC fifth wave (child aged 7) and sixth wave (child aged 11); survey waves fielded on a rolling basis
population.selection: children enrolled in the DNBC (women pregnant 1996-2002, roughly 10% of births) who responded to the fifth and/or sixth survey wave and have a completed SDQ and school starting age; the survey sample has higher birth weight, fewer non-Western children and more educated, richer and older parents than the population (Table 1), and the authors state the survey data are not representative

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

lhs: born on or after the January 1 cutoff
given: day of birth relative to the January 1 cutoff (smooth function; local sample within 30 days)

implies_edges.to: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

implies_edges.to: born on or after the January 1 cutoff

key_assumptions.assumption: The local linear/polynomial specification in the forcing variable and the 30-day bandwidth are adequate (functional form and bandwidth choice)
key_assumptions.supported_by: results from various specifications and bandwidths (20 to 170 days, first- to third-order polynomials) in Figures A2 and A3

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on participation and response in the DNBC survey waves, which is nonrandom; the authors assume this does not threaten internal validity because participation is balanced at the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure A1 shows no sign of a jump in attrition around the cutoff; participation is balanced around the birthday threshold; the authors concede an external-validity caveat

implies_edges.from: DNBC participation and response in the age-7/age-11 survey wave

key_assumptions.assumption: Mother-reported SDQ ratings are not driven by reference-group (rater) bias, i.e. the ratings are not merely relative to the child's classroom peers
key_assumptions.supported_by: Elder (2010) finds parental assessments are not subject to these biases; the authors also split the sample by whether the child has an older sibling and condition on classmates' average school starting age (Table 7)

threats_discussed: manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 threshold
nonrandom selection into the DNBC survey and nonrandom nonresponse to the last survey waves (external validity)
the ITT contrast conflates a higher school starting age with fewer years of formal schooling at the time of observation
reference-group (rater) bias in mother-reported SDQ ratings
choice of functional form and bandwidth
localness of the RD estimand and the LATE/complier interpretation of the fuzzy design
multiple hypothesis testing across the 12 core outcomes (six SDQ measures at two ages)
robustness_checks: estimates with and without the full covariate set (Table 2 and Table 4, columns 1 and 3 vs 2 and 4)
McCrary density test of the running variable (Figure 2) and histogram of birth dates in survey and population data (Figure A1)
covariate balance regressions (Table A1) and balance of the covariate index predicting each outcome (Table 3)
placebo regressions on pretreatment developmental measures reported at 18 months (Table A2)
bandwidth sensitivity from 20 to 170 days with first-, second- and third-order polynomials (Figures A2 and A3)
sample splits by gender, parental education, parental income and birth weight (Tables 5 and 6)
splits by older-sibling status and a specification conditioning on classmates' average school starting age (Table 7)
binary abnormal and borderline outcomes (Table 8)
complier diagnostics following Bertanha and Imbens (2014) (Figures 5 and 6)
unresolved_confounders: years of formal schooling at the time of observation is collinear with school starting age in the ITT contrast; the authors argue the role of years of schooling can be deprecated rather than ruling it out
possible reference-group (rater) bias in mother-reported SDQ ratings, which the authors assess only indirectly
nonrandom nonresponse to the last DNBC survey waves (respondents tended to be more affluent)

population.period: DNBC fifth wave (child aged 7) and sixth wave (child aged 11); survey waves fielded on a rolling basis
population.selection: children enrolled in the DNBC (women pregnant 1996-2002, roughly 10% of births) who responded to the fifth and/or sixth survey wave and have a completed SDQ and school starting age; the survey sample has higher birth weight, fewer non-Western children and more educated, richer and older parents than the population (Table 1), and the authors state the survey data are not representative

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in school starting age around the threshold is 'as good as randomized': predetermined child and family traits (and the potential outcomes) are continuous at the cutoff conditional on a smooth function of the day of birth
key_assumptions.supported_by: covariate balance regressions (Table A1: no clear sign of jumps; joint F-statistic 0.778, p = 0.606), balance of the covariate index predicting each SDQ outcome (Table 3), and placebo regressions on pretreatment 18-month developmental measures (Table A2)

key_assumptions.assumption: Mother-reported SDQ ratings are not driven by reference-group (rater) bias, i.e. the ratings are not merely relative to the child's classroom peers

covariate balance regressions (Table A1) and balance of the covariate index predicting each outcome (Table 3)

bandwidth sensitivity from 20 to 170 days with first-, second- and third-order polynomials (Figures A2 and A3)

anchor_quote.text: The significant drop in the inattention/hyperactivity measure to the right of the threshold indicates that, even when all are taking the treatment, compliers have lower levels of inattention/hyperactivity than always-takers.

claims.statement: Using the age-11 data, the profile among children who did not take up the older school start implies that those who never choose to take up a delayed school start have low levels of inattention/hyperactivity (a high degree of self-regulation) relative to the population that would comply when encouraged.

treatment.label: SSO: a binary indicator for older school starting age (first entering kindergarten at age 6.5 years or older)

definition.value: Binary indicator for an older school starting age, defined as first entering kindergarten at age 6.5 years or older; used for the Bertanha and Imbens (2014) complier diagnostic.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten

outcome.label: Standardized SDQ inattention/hyperactivity score at age 11

definition.value: Sum of the five mother-rated SDQ items linked to the inattention/hyperactivity subscale (range 0 to 10), standardized using the full population in each survey wave. population.description: Children in the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC) born within 30 days before or after the January 1 school-entry cutoff, with information on school starting age and a completed SDQ in the sixth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 11 years old; split by the binary treatment SSO (entering kindergarten at age 6.5 years or older)

identification.source_of_variation: The Danish rule that children are supposed to enroll in school in the calendar year in which they turn 6, which makes school starting age jump discontinuously between children born December 31 and January 1; compliance is partial, so the design is a 'fuzzy' RD in the exact date of birth
identification.instrument: 1(day_i >= 0), an indicator for being born on January 1 or later, instrumenting school starting age

key_assumptions.assumption: No empirically meaningful manipulation of the date of birth around the January 1 cutoff: the density of births is continuous through the threshold
key_assumptions.supported_by: McCrary (2008) density test (Figure 2; the jump is estimated to be -0.018 with a standard error of 0.086) and a histogram of birth dates local to the threshold in survey and population data (Figure A1)

claims.statement: A 1-year increase in school starting age reduces the standardized SDQ total difficulties score at age 7 by about 0.6 standard deviations.

treatment.label: School starting age (age at kindergarten entry, in years)

register_source.value: DNBC fifth survey wave (the respondent was asked when the child started kindergarten), matched to population data in the Danish administrative registers and Ministry of Education records; no register code is given

definition.value: The age at which the child enters kindergarten (grade zero, in Danish 'Boernehaveklasse'), in years, identified from the mother's report in the DNBC fifth wave; compulsory education begins in grade zero in August of the year in which the child turns 6, and complying children born January 1 have a school starting age one year higher than children born one day earlier.

timing.value: at entry into kindergarten, around age 6 to 6.5 (survey sample mean 6.48 years, SD 0.67)

outcome.label: Standardized SDQ total difficulties score at age 7

definition.value: Sum of the four difficulties subscales (emotional symptoms, conduct problems, inattention/hyperactivity, peer problems), excluding the pro-social score; range 0 to 40. Each of the 25 mother-rated items is scored 0, 1 or 2 and each subscore is the sum of its five linked items. Standardized using the full population in each survey wave so coefficients are effect sizes.

timing.value: mother-rated in the fifth DNBC survey wave, when the focal child was 7 years old; raters are asked to consider the last 6 months

units.value: standard deviations of the standardized SDQ score per 1-year increase in school starting age

magnitude.interpretation: the paper words this as 'significantly improved mental health', and the conclusions put it as reducing the overall difficulties score by at least 0.5 SD
